subject: biology
title: Nutrient cycles and decomposition
key_idea: Nutrients are recycled in ecosystems. Microorganisms are vital: saprobionts decompose dead material, and bacteria change nitrogen between its forms. The carbon cycle links photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition.

blocks.text: Dead plants, animals and waste contain elements that other organisms need. Microorganisms break these down and return the elements to the environment.

items.meaning: A decomposer, mostly bacteria and fungi, that feeds on dead organic matter by external digestion.
The breakdown of dead organic matter into simple inorganic substances.

items: Saprobionts secrete **enzymes** onto dead material. This is extracellular digestion.
They absorb the soluble products, such as sugars and amino acids, for their own use.
They respire, releasing carbon dioxide, and they release ammonia, ions and minerals into the soil.
Decomposition is faster when it is warm, moist and has plenty of oxygen.
Saprobionts digest dead material using extracellular enzymes and absorb the products.
Their activity recycles carbon, nitrogen and other elements for producers to use again.

blocks.text: Plants and animals need nitrogen to make proteins and nucleic acids. Most of the nitrogen is in the air as N₂, which they cannot use directly. Bacteria convert it between several forms.

diagram.alt: The nitrogen cycle as a loop.
steps: Plants take up nitrate and make protein
Plants and animals die: ammonification returns ammonium ions
Denitrification turns nitrate back into N₂ gas

rows: Nitrogen gas is converted to ammonia or ammonium ions
Saprobionts break down proteins and urea in dead matter and waste into ammonia and ammonium ions
Ammonium ions are oxidised to nitrite (Nitrosomonas), then nitrite is oxidised to nitrate (Nitrobacter)
Nitrate is converted to nitrogen gas, in waterlogged soil with little oxygen

items: Plants absorb **nitrate** ions through their roots and use them to make amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids.
Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
Nitrification needs oxygen, so it is slow in waterlogged soil, where denitrification is favoured.
Nitrogen is cycled by fixation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification, all carried out by microorganisms.
Plants take up nitrate; denitrification returns nitrogen to the air.

blocks.text: Carbon moves between the air, living things and the ground. Biological and physical processes both play a part.

items: **Photosynthesis** removes carbon dioxide from the air and builds carbon compounds in plants.
Animals eat plants and other animals, passing carbon compounds along food chains.
**Respiration** by all organisms returns carbon dioxide to the air.
**Decomposition** by saprobionts breaks down dead material and releases carbon dioxide by respiration.
Some carbon is locked away as fossil fuels, peat and limestone. Burning fossil fuels (combustion) releases CO₂.
Physical and chemical effects: carbon dioxide dissolves in the oceans, and marine organisms form shells of calcium carbonate.
Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air; respiration, decomposition and combustion put it back.
Decomposition by microorganisms keeps carbon cycling instead of being locked in dead material.

checks.q: Name the process by which Rhizobium bacteria help legumes, and state its product.
checks.a: Nitrogen fixation: nitrogen gas from the air is converted to ammonia or ammonium ions.

checks.q: Describe the roles of microorganisms in the nitrogen cycle.
checks.a: Saprobionts carry out ammonification, releasing ammonium from dead matter; nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate; nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn N₂ into ammonium; denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into N₂.

checks.q: Explain how saprobionts return carbon to the atmosphere.
checks.a: They secrete enzymes to digest dead organic matter, absorb the products and respire them, releasing carbon dioxide into the air.

items: Nutrients are also recycled in the phosphorus cycle. Phosphate ions in rocks and soil are taken up by plants, passed along food chains and returned by decomposers.
**Mycorrhizae** are associations between fungi and plant roots. The fungal hyphae increase the surface area for the uptake of water and inorganic ions, and the plant gives the fungus sugars.
Harvesting plants and removing livestock takes nitrates and phosphates out of the system. Natural fertilisers (manure) and artificial fertilisers replace them.
**Leaching** washes soluble nitrates and phosphates out of the soil into water.
**Eutrophication**: nutrients in the water cause algal bloom, which blocks light. Plants die, decomposers multiply and use up the oxygen, and aerobic organisms such as fish die.
The names of individual bacteria are not required.
Knowledge of the carbon cycle can reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide: protect forests and peat bogs, plant new forests, and use biofuels in place of fossil fuels.
**Time of death** of a mammal can be worked out from the extent of decomposition, the stage of succession on the body, forensic entomology, body temperature and muscle contraction.
The body cools after death, and the temperature drop shows how long ago it died.
**Rigor mortis**, the stiffening of muscles, starts a few hours after death and later passes. The degree of contraction gives an estimate of time.
Forensic entomology uses the stage of the life cycle of insects, such as blowfly larvae, found on the body.
Different species colonise a body in a set order as it decomposes, which is a succession.

Know the named microorganisms in the nitrogen cycle: Azotobacter (free-living nitrogen fixer), Rhizobium (nitrogen fixer in nodules), Nitrosomonas (ammonium to nitrite) and Nitrobacter (nitrite to nitrate).
Know the role of decomposers in recycling nutrients.
